properties.foundation_analysis: The subterranean strata beneath Edinburgh's West End consist of early Carboniferous sedimentary sequences of the Strathclyde Group (sandstones, siltstones, and thin mudstones/shales), uncomformably overlying volcanic intrusions and basaltic plugs such as those forming Castle Rock and Arthur's Seat visible on the eastern horizon. The primary construction material defining the entire vista is indigenous Carboniferous Craigleith and Hailes sandstone—a quartz-rich, pale greyish-buff to light olive-brown sandstone known for exceptional density and silica cementation. Mortar beds throughout the Victorian and late Georgian ashlar construction are formulated from traditional non-hydraulic to weakly hydraulic lime mortar aggregate mixtures. Subterranean moisture management relies on natural subterranean gradients draining towards the Water of Leith basin, with extensive subterranean basement lightwells (areas) lined with droved stone retaining walls.

properties.primary_surfacing: Engineered roadway and paved pedestrian curbs
properties.wear_characteristics: Authentic environmental patina and drainage grading

properties.botanical_analysis: Urban mature deciduous trees punctuate private cathedral grounds, garden enclosures, and flanking avenue sidewalks. Botanical species include mature European sycamores (*Acer pseudoplatanus*), English oaks (*Quercus robur*), London plane trees (*Platanus x acerifolia*), and Wych elms (*Ulmus glabra*), rendered with full leafy canopies, distinct organic branch architecture, and healthy urban turfgrass borders within the cathedral perimeter grounds.

properties.architectural_summary: The central visual anchor is St Mary's Episcopal Cathedral (designed by Sir George Gilbert Scott, consecrated 1879), an Early English/Gothic Revival cruciform cathedral featuring a towering 90m central crossing spire with decorative broaches, paired 84m western flanking towers ("Barbara" and "Mary", completed 1917), steeply pitched slate rooflines, clear cross-gabled transepts, flying buttresses, and tall lancet clerestory windows. Surrounding the cathedral is the high-density Victorian and late Georgian West End residential/civic grid, predominantly 3-to-4 storey plus raised basement and attic dormer terraced tenements and crescent townhouses (e.g., Palmerston Place, Eglinton Crescent). All photogrammetry distortion is rectified: wall planes are plumbed to absolute gravity-vertical; long continuous slate mansards, chimneys stacks, stone balustrades, string courses, and ashlar cornices form rigid, planar linear horizontals.
